title: Nanquan Cuts the Cat
author: Zhiyu
excerpt: (Original text from the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

inline.s: (Original text from the Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
“Nanquan Cuts the Cat”
is a famous Chan gong’an that has been analyzed countless times over the centuries. Here it is annotated as follows:
the Master
Nanquan
came upon the east and west halls quarreling over a cat
and addressed the assembly
If you can speak, you will save the cat;
if you cannot speak, I will cut it in two.
The assembly had no reply,
so the Master cut it in two.]

The east hall and the west hall were quarreling over a cat. Nanquan came upon them and said to the assembly: “Tell me your view of this matter; if you speak rightly, you will save the cat, and if you speak wrongly, I will cut the cat in two.” No one had a word to say, so Nanquan cut the cat in two with one stroke.

[Nanquan] Chan Master Puyuan of Mount Nanquan in Chizhou during the Tang dynasty, a Dharma heir of Mazu. [Dharma heir] One who inherits the Dharma lineage. [West hall, east hall] The west hall refers to former abbots and retired elders of other monasteries who were staying as guests in this monastery; the east hall refers to the former abbot and retired elders of this very monastery. In the Chan community, the east is the host’s position and the west is the guest’s position. Since the former abbot and elders of this monastery are its old hosts, they dwell in the east hall; while former abbots and elders of other monasteries who come are treated as guests, and so dwell in the west hall.

[To speak or not to speak] Clearly, “to speak or not to speak” refers to one’s view of the quarrel over the cat, not to one’s view of the cutting of the cat. [The assembly had no reply, so the Master cut it in two] Both halls were full of seasoned Chan practitioners, yet not one of them was a person of clear understanding — this Nanquan had never anticipated! A word once spoken cannot be overtaken even by a team of four horses; left with no choice, he had to cut the cat. [Chan practitioner] Also called a chanhezi, one who practices Chan. [This Nanquan had never anticipated] Who would have thought that these people had practiced Chan their whole lives — and what had they practiced! Therefore Xuedou Chongxian wrote in a verse:
“The monks of both halls are all counterfeit Chan practitioners
(the monks of both east and west halls are all sham practitioners)

(The Blue Cliff Record) [Counterfeit Chan practitioner] An abbreviation of “fabricated Chan practitioner,” a term of the Chan community. [So the Master cut it in two] Nanquan had assumed that the two halls must harbor true practitioners, and wanted to dramatize the incident to teach the assembly; unexpectedly the pretense turned real. Alas! Alas!
[When Zhaozhou returned from outside
the Master related the previous words to him. Zhaozhou then took off his sandal and placed it on his head
to show that things were upside down
and walked out. The Master said
If you had been here just now,
you would have saved the cat.

Later Zhaozhou (Chan Master Congshen) returned from outside. Nanquan related to him what he had said before (“If you can speak, you will save the cat; if you cannot speak, I will cut it in two” — clearly, “to speak or not to speak” refers to one’s view of the quarrel over the cat, not to one’s view of the cutting of the cat!) — testing Zhaozhou to see how he would speak. Zhaozhou took off his sandal, placed it on his head, and walked out (a wordless reply: quarreling over a cat is clinging to illusion as reality — upside down! Note that at this moment Zhaozhou did not know whether the cat had been cut or not; he was merely answering his teacher’s test). Nanquan said: “If you had been here just now, you would have saved the cat” — approving that his view of the quarrel over the cat was right, and sighing: if only you had been here then!

[Chan Master Zhaozhou Congshen (778–897)] A native of Caozhou (present-day Heze, Shandong), he was a master whose fame resounded through past and present in the history of Chan. He became a monk in childhood and later received the Dharma from Chan Master Nanquan Puyuan, becoming the fourth-generation heir after the Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng. In the eleventh year of the Dazhong reign of the Tang dynasty (857), the eighty-year-old Master Congshen arrived in Zhaozhou (present-day Zhao County, Hebei), and at the urging of the faithful took up residence at Avalokiteshvara Monastery, where he spread the Dharma and taught Chan for forty years. Monks and laypeople alike revered him as a model of the monastic community, calling him the “Ancient Buddha of Zhaozhou”; he lived to the age of 120. [Taking off the sandal and placing it on the head] A sandal belongs on the feet, but he put it on his head — a wordless answer: upside down (clinging to illusion as reality). [Approval] To affirm a disciple’s attainment and give it praise and sanction.
[Upside down] Clinging to illusion as reality. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“All sentient beings, since beginningless time,
have been subject to every kind of inversion
, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another
(like a lost traveler who mistakes east, south, west, and north)

, falsely taking the four great elements as the form of their own body, and the reflections of the six sense-objects as the form of their own mind. ... Because of this false existence, they revolve in birth and death.”
(see
An Elucidation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

[Four great elements] All material forms in the world are composed of the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, and so they are called “great” — the great element of earth, the great element of water, the great element of fire, and the great element of wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water moisture, fire warmth, and wind movement. Here the four great elements refer to the human body.

[Reflections of the six sense-objects] The various thoughts produced when the six sense-faculties encounter the six sense-objects; since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the reflections of the six sense-objects — the phantom images produced by contact with the six sense-objects.
Commentary:

The whole world is one great quarrel — even those who cultivate the Way are quarreling! The cat was cut, and the dispute was stilled. Yet the cat was cut but the quarrelsome mind was not, and so there remains a hundred thousand miles before the attainment of the Way. Hence it is said: it is finished, yet not finished.
A discourse says:

Those who cultivate the Way all know that the self-nature is the true self, the body is a lodging-house, the mind is the reflection of the six sense-objects, and the world is a dream of samsara. But whether one has truly awakened to the self-nature as the true self is tested by one standard:
that illusion no longer holds power
(one no longer clings to illusion as reality)
This is the grandmotherly kindness with which Master Nanquan gave his warning.

[The mind is the reflection of the six sense-objects] The mind is the phantom image produced when the six sense-faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) encounter the six sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas). When a person dies, the six sense-faculties perish, and this mind of reflected sense-objects ceases to be.

[Granny] An old grandmother — in the Chan community the term describes a teacher who, like a grandmother, admonishes earnestly and repeatedly. The teachings of Huangbo Xiyun and Dayu Shouzhi were so earnest and untiring that people used to say: “Huangbo is a granny, and Dayu is a chatterbox.”
